en: The *Sūtra on the Great Dhāraṇī of the Ambrosial Flavor Bestowed upon Hungry Ghosts*, spoken by the Buddha and translated by the Venerable Bodhimukha: Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was dwelling on a solitary peak, preaching the Dharma within an ocean-like assembly.
On Mount Ta, at the site of enlightenment within the Golden Vajra-Wheel Peak Lūkeśa-pāla,

surrounded by an incalculable and ineffable assembly of the fourfold community, the World-Honored One sat upon a golden eight-sided lion throne and was about to conclude his exposition of the Vaipulya Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the evil realms...
Because he wishes to expound for the sake of all classes of sentient beings the *Kṣaṇabhadra-mahāpariśuddha-pañcara-dhāraṇī*—
translated into Chinese as the *Dhāraṇī of the Great Maṇḍala Assembly of Ambrosial Flavor Bestowed upon Hungry Ghosts*—
which is the supreme, great compassionate, secret, and virtuous gateway, he secretly emits a moon from within his heart.
The light of the color of a refined maṇi jewel is named "Moon-Loving Compassionate Light.
From the Peak of Existence above down to the Avīci Hell below, everything therein is completely transparent and clear, like a crystal mirror, such that all things are seen as reflected images;
even throughout the ten directions, there is nowhere it does not pervade. Thus he proclaimed:
The great assembly said:
"Good sons! Observe for a moment how you receive bodies within the six realms of existence and undergo all manner of suffering and affliction."
Thereupon, the great assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, beheld this event and together cried out:
"Indeed! We have seen it!"
The Buddha said:
"The eight sufferings of the world are hardly worth mentioning;
the calamities of the six realms of existence are truly terrifying."
The reason for this is that those people in the world do not believe in sin and merit, slander the existence of cause and effect, are deluded and ignorant, and are stingy, greedy, and envious.
After their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell as retribution, where they fully experience inconceivable suffering.
Emerging from hell, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), where they undergo various distinctions of retribution due to their accumulated evil karma.
Because of their evil karma, they receive the bodies of thirty-six kinds of hungry ghosts, namely:
*pīluotuo* ghosts (translated in Chinese as "hungry ghosts"), *cheyie* ghosts (translated in Chinese as "shadow ghosts"), and *jianduo* ghosts.
The *gandharva* (translated in Chinese as "Fragrance-Eating Ghost"), the *puṣpa-bhūta* (translated in Chinese as "Flower-Eating Hungry Ghost"),
the *garbhaya* (translated as "Womb-Eating Ghost"), the *aśucya* (translated as "Impurity-Eating Ghost"),
the *vāta* (translated as "Wind-Eating Ghost"), the *udghāra* (translated as "Essence-Eating Ghost"), and the *dhārā-jita* (translated as "Anger").
The *duṣṭacitta* spirits; the *citra* spirits; the *varuṇa* spirits who consume sacrificial offerings;
the *vetāla* spirits who consume the life-span of humans; the *śiśumāra* spirits who consume flesh, fat, and the like;
the *sarpadaṃṣṭra* spirits, also known as those who consume newborn infants; and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* spirits, also known as the "strange ones."
The Pūtanā spirits, whose bodies smell like burnt bones;
the Kumbhāṇḍas, the Śālakaṭaṅkaṭas, the Piśācas, and the Vāyus—also known as "guardians of latrines"—who wait for human excrement as food.

In this manner, even within light or heavy cavities and the like, because of their profound evil karma, the fierce fires of hunger and thirst burn, and the flames of jealousy blaze; they constantly crave food and drink, thinking only of water and broth, knowing nothing else, and undergo various forms of bitter suffering that are beyond description.
Having received this body, it is like a great mass of fire; its form is emaciated, withered, and parched, its limbs are thin and weak, and its feet are like overturned basins.
The skin and flesh are dry, and the blood vessels are withered and exhausted, resembling dried meat jerky.
Their bellies are distended and bloated, shaped like drums;
their throats are as narrow as the point of a needle, through which neither breath nor air can pass, and within them there is always a fierce fire burning.
Their heads span five Mount Merus in length and breadth, and the blazing flames never cease for even a moment.
Whenever they move their bodies, blazing fires erupt; they are constantly tormented by hunger, thirst, and great conflagrations that burn and afflict both body and mind.
They run hither and thither, wailing and crying out, seeking food and drink.
If they see delicious food and wish to go toward it, the power of their craving causes that exquisite delicacy to transform into pus and blood, overflowing with foul stench.
Even if they see a great river or cool spring water and wish to go there to drink, the water deities strike them with iron staffs.
If there is no one to guard it, the cool, clear water will transform into flames.
Furthermore, eagles, vultures, crows, kites, hawks, falcons, and other birds with iron beaks will remain there to peck at one's eyes.
Poisonous and fierce beasts—starving tigers, famished wolves, wild snakes, and bronze dogs—crawl, claw, seize, and pounce upon them, their suffering beyond words.
Their bodies are mangled and torn, their hair and fur bristling and standing on end; at the tip of every single hair, they are bitten and eaten by eighteen thousand venomous and wicked insects.

Because the various hungry ghosts are so intensely oppressed by hunger, their minds of anger increase further; they harm one another, splitting open skulls to extract the marrow and devouring each other in turn.
For five hundred kalpas, they have not even heard the names of water or drink, let alone having seen them.
Such suffering and affliction are beyond comparison and cannot be known through calculation. To state it briefly:
even if one has fully experienced such embodied existence for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, only when one's black karma is diminished and exhausted can one finally attain liberation.
Having left that place, they further become various kinds of insects and beasts, constantly dwelling in enclosures and latrines, or crouching in lower currents and foul-smelling, impure places.
"O sons of good family!

These hungry ghosts all arose because in their previous lives they were deluded and perverse, tormented by greed and bound by attachments; their minds were as hard as iron, finding pleasure only in scheming and plundering others without ever knowing contentment.
They provide nothing at all for their parents, wives, or children;
they regard the instructions of their teachers as if they were excrement and filth;
and they do not bestow gifts upon their female servants or close friends.

Such a miserly person does not contemplate impermanence; they guard and cherish their wealth, saying they will live for a hundred years, and furthermore, they teach others to greedily seek out and hoard it.

Unaware of impermanence, they are pursued by old age and sickness; when the body encounters a grave illness and they know for themselves that they will not last long, they constantly think silently to themselves:
"During my life, I labored diligently to seek wealth."
If, after my death, these wicked people consume my wealth and property, it will be like swallowing fierce flames; if they dwell in my house and residence, it will be like staying in a dark chamber.

While he was thinking this, due to his evil karma, rākṣasas and hell-wardens transformed themselves into tormentors; they seized his means of subsistence and went to the place of the offender, where they burned him with fire, yet the offender felt joy.
Due to these causes and conditions, within the path of evil karma, the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) appear.
First, the element of wind moves; the signs of warmth and heat are lost, and various winds that are yellow and cold are thereby set in motion.

Because of the agitation caused by malignant winds, the sinews and veins become withered and parched (the character for *dǎn* is pronounced *tā-dàn-fǎn*); the mouth becomes dry; the face and eyes become sunken and the teeth recede; the entire body turns withered and yellow; the abdomen swells and becomes coarse and bloated; blue and yellow veins protrude; food and drink are not digested; the body becomes emaciated; the mouth is bitter and the urine is yellow; the eyes lose their luster and see only flames; the throat is constricted and swollen with urgency; gasping breath fills the chest; a foul stench emanates from the heart; it rises to the throat; the voice is choked and short of breath; the whole body is covered in sores and leprosy; pus and blood are putrid and rotting as they endure great agony.
As he was about to pass away, he again formed this thought:
"I would rather obtain an iron ball to burn through my throat,
or obtain a great mass of fire to sit within."
"Furthermore, I have found a dark place that is free from blazing flames and can cure cold ailments;
would that not be most pleasant!

At that moment, the hell-warden transformed himself into a skilled physician and conjured an iron ball that appeared like a large medicinal pill, placing it in his mouth and commanding him to hold it there tightly.
Furthermore, he transforms a great carriage into a golden lotus flower, upon which sits a youth holding a fly-whisk and performing a dance.
When the sick person sees this, a mind of attachment arises:
"This transformation is warm; it will surely remove my cold."
He immediately went toward it and, his breath ceasing, his life ended, and he was reborn in the Iron Ball Cave within the Avīci Hell.
"In this hell, this is the place of extreme suffering and affliction for those in the realm of hungry ghosts."
There is an iron mountain, twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal in all dimensions.
On the eastern side of that mountain is a small hole, the size of a Magadha-measure, from which only black smoke issues forth.
Once they have entered therein, sword-worms and blade-worms devour their bodies, and smoke agitates their eyes so that they cannot see the flames.

They run about within the surrounding barriers, striking their heads against iron mountains until their brains shatter and marrow flows out like a broken jar of curd. Iron balls enter through the crown of their heads and emerge from their feet; in brief, they die in a single thought-moment and are reborn in a single thought-moment.

When their transgressions are exhausted, they are reborn among the ghosts who feed on mucus and saliva, and among those who feed on pus and blood; from there they pass on successively to be born as deities of the latrine, where they seek out impurities and take them to eat and drink.
When the retribution for these offenses is completed, they are born among animals, mostly taking the bodies of dogs and the like.
Once this is finished, they are again born into poverty, solitary and destitute, adorned with abscesses, leprosy, malignant sores, chronic coughs, consumption, and all manner of misfortunes.
Such a person, loathsome to behold, dies of cold and hunger;
seeing such a form and receiving such a reward—whether beautiful or ugly—one’s body hair stands on end even upon hearing of it, let alone seeing it with one's own eyes!
Therefore, you all should give rise to great compassion and rescue them from their suffering and distress. Why is this?

All these hungry ghosts were, in the past, your own parents, brothers, sisters, and other kin; yet, due to their inverted views and ignorance, they refused to seek the bliss of transcendence and, out of attachment to the three realms, committed a multitude of sins.
Impelled by the power of karma, they are born among the hungry ghosts, where they are tormented by intersecting sufferings with no time of escape, forever losing the human body.
Having lost the human body, they remain far removed from virtuous friends.
Because they distance themselves from virtuous friends, the heavy veil of the net of doubt remains, and they shall never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, you should know that they are truly pitiable; one must uproot their suffering and distress so that they may obtain liberation.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Candraprema (Moon-Love), who had long since cultivated the ocean of practices of great compassion.

Having witnessed this event, his body trembled, his sinews and veins were pulled with intense pain, and he was overwhelmed by the force of his sorrowful emotion. Rising from his seat, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet; his eyes filled with tears of grief as he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha: "Alas!..."
“Bhagavān! We pray that you will teach us the methods for rescue and protection, so that many may find peace and security!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Candraprabha:
“Excellent, Great Being!
You are truly one of great compassion, a practitioner of great compassion.”
Out of compassion for all beings, you have asked me this question.
Listen well,
son of good family!

I possess a supreme gate of great compassion called the *Dhāraṇī-mukha*, titled "The Ambrosial Dharma of the Great Assembly of the Kṣaṇabhadra Great Maṇḍala. It is inconceivable, endowed with great compassion, and possesses great majestic power. It can shatter the vast mountains of karma belonging to those in the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts; it can also cause Bodhisattvas to swiftly attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s Only Son, and further achieve one hundred and ten kinds of great compassionate minds. It enables the holder to realize in this very body the *Dhāraṇī* of the Sovereign King of the Summit of the Wheel of Great Compassion and the Samādhi-gate of the Indestructible Treasury of Great Compassion.
"Good son!

This great divine mantra can extinguish the intense fires of hunger and thirst of the hungry ghosts, bestowing upon them the cool, sweet flavor of ambrosia, and ensuring that they will certainly and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Just as the moon at night can dispel the oppressive heat, so too is this dhāraṇī.
You should fix your mindfulness and listen with single-minded attention; do not allow it to be forgotten or lost.
I shall now explain it. "Good son!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, boys, girls, or any among the humans and devas who wish to receive and uphold this method of skillful means, they must summon and invite all the hungry ghosts and spirits of the six realms throughout the entirety of the ten directions."
One should form this thought:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Dharmāya!"
Homage to the Saṅgha!
Homage to the Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni!
Homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas dwelling securely upon the great earth!
Homage to all dragon deities and benevolent spirits!
May you, through your majestic spiritual power, grant your compassionate protection and assistance.

I now invoke and invite all sentient beings of the six realms of existence throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space; by the majestic spiritual power of the Triple Gem, may they all come to my presence.
Having spoken thus, he turned his face toward the east and immediately recited the mantra for summoning and inviting seven times.
At that time, the World-Honored One then proclaimed the Dhāraṇī-mantra for summoning and inviting for Candraprabha.
He then spoke the mantra:
"Namo *buburi* tathāgatāya. The Buddha told Candraprabha:

"Once they have been summoned, all the hungry ghosts, spirits, and deities of the six realms throughout the ten directions will gather there; they will gaze upon the practitioner as if seeing their own parents."
At that time, the practitioner should give rise to a heart of great compassion and say to them: "Listen well!
I shall now open your throats with this dhāraṇī, bestowing upon you coolness, softness, and joy, so that you may freely partake of the delicious flavor of ambrosia."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the Kaṇṭhaviśodhana Dhāraṇī mantra, saying:

“Oṃ, pūri, kaṇṭhe, tattakāta. Having recited this divine dhāraṇī mantra seven times, by the power of this mantra, the throats of these various spirits will become permeable for breath, their fierce fires will be extinguished, and they will no longer suffer pain or affliction; their bodies and minds will be at ease.
At that time, the practitioner should first offer water.

One who wishes to offer water should, every morning or at midday, take a handful of pure water, face the east, recite the mantra over it seven times, and scatter it toward the east, letting it remain suspended in the air.
By the power of this dhāraṇī, every single drop of that water falling to the ground transforms into ten *shu* of celestial ambrosial nectar.
All the spirits and ghosts are fully satiated and filled with immeasurable joy.
At that time, for the sake of Candraprabha, the World-Honored One spoke this *dhāraṇī* for consecrating water, saying:
"Namo suluva-ye, tākathadaye, tatteha, sulu sulu, parāsulu, svāhā. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, saying:
"Good son!"
This is called the "Dhāraṇī Divine Mantra for Bestowing the Ambrosial Beverage.

Furthermore, if any humans or devas wish to bestow food upon [the practitioner], they must, every day before the time of their midday meal, use an excellent and most superior vessel—whether a bowl made of gold, silver, copper, iron, brass, stone, lead, tin, or vessels of lapis lazuli, crystal, shell, jade, or the like; or, if these are unavailable, provided it is simply a clean wooden, stone, or earthenware vessel, or even one made of a gourd or calabash—and fill it to the brim with milk and curd.
If there is no milk or curd, pure water may also be used.

Take whatever food and drink is available—whether it be milk-rice, rice from non-glutinous rice or barley, or cakes, leavened flour, gruel, and so forth—and place it in a vessel; do not include any leafy vegetables.
Beneath a single cool and shady tree, first recite the mantra for summoning and inviting, and next recite the mantra for opening the throat, as previously described;
having recited the mantra over the food in the vessel seven times, pour it out beneath the tree.

At that time, by the majestic power of the dhāraṇī, all the hungry ghosts of the ten directions were able to eat; moreover, the food did not transform into pus or blood, and there were no prohibitions, so they ate and drank to their heart’s content until they were fully satisfied. Their hunger and thirst, which had been like fire, were extinguished; their bodies became peaceful and happy, free from all pain and affliction.

Furthermore, there are cool, soft, and gentle breezes that come to touch their bodies; the defilement of stinginess is extinguished, and they are free from the suffering of bodily heat, remaining in a state of profound bliss.
All the long body hairs and malevolent insects fall away, and no poisonous or wicked birds or beasts come to harm or destroy them; their minds are courageous and joyful.

By these causes and conditions, their retribution for sins will be exhausted and they shall emerge from it, being reborn among humans and devas to experience the supreme, subtle, and wondrous bliss of the Honored Ones, with extraordinary excellence and sovereignty.
You should know that such persons can be praised only by Buddhas and Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One then proclaimed the *dhāraṇī* mantra for bestowing the food of ambrosia, saying:

"Namo sabhā tathāgatāya | namo ākṣate | samala samala. When Śākyamuni Buddha had finished speaking this supreme *dhāraṇī* mantra of Great Compassion, at that moment, the earth and heavens shook in six ways.

Throughout this trichiliocosm, all was filled with radiance; celestial jewel-flowers fell in dense clouds, while celestial jewel-incense, necklaces, and musical instruments descended like a torrential rain.

At that moment, throughout all the uninterrupted realms of the six destinies, the instruments for inflicting punishment and suffering struck against one another, their sounds resonating and proclaiming the teachings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and liberation.
In the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals, they were crushed and destroyed.
All the sinners recognized their own past lives; they felt a sense of relief and joy, as if entering the third dhyāna.
Within this assembly, there were those who attained the first fruit up to the fruit of arhatship, and immeasurable humans and devas resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Candraprabha and the great assembly:
"This dhāraṇī is difficult even to hear, let alone to behold!"
All the Tathāgatas of the past and future, numbering in the millions, have together proclaimed it; I, Śākyamuni, now likewise reveal and proclaim it for you.
O son of good family!

If gods and humans uphold this according to the Dharma, yet are still tormented by ghosts and spirits or by hunger and thirst, and suffer untimely or violent deaths, then it cannot be called the "Dhāraṇī of Supreme Great Compassion."

Why is this? This dhāraṇī is like the sovereign maṇi-jewel, capable of fulfilling all wishes and aspirations; it is also like the bright moon, able to cause the udumbara flower to bloom with radiant beauty.
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who does not cling to his own happiness but rescues others from their suffering, who cultivates great compassion through habitual practice, who brings benefit and peace to all, and who carries out his actions in accordance with the Dharma—such a person is truly a bodhisattva of great compassion."

This person has already practiced the conduct of Avalokiteśvara; all Buddhas extend their hands to stroke their heads, all honored Bodhisattvas cherish and protect them, all worthy sages regard them as their own children, and all devas, nāgas, and spirits attend to and guard them.
Candrakānta!
You should know that the merit of this person is equal to that of the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Why is this?

If this good man, who is a courageous and resolute individual, practices daily and gives food on even a single day, all the hungry ghosts within one world-system will obtain food to eat; if he gives food for many days, all the hungry ghosts throughout the six realms of the ten directions will be completely satiated.
The mass of merit obtained by such a bodhisattva is inconceivable and difficult to measure; without perceiving or knowing it, they spontaneously attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!

If one merely praises, recites, copies, or transcribes this dhāraṇī, that person will transcend the subtle cycle of birth and death for sixty billion kalpas of the mundane world; how much more so for those who practice according to the Dharma without interruption."
"Good son!
I now speak to you clearly:

if this mantra-holder, before the presence of Maitreya Buddha, does not receive the definitive prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and subsequently attain Buddhahood in succession within this Bhadrakalpa, then I would have deceived sentient beings, and all the sūtras and dharmas I have preached since attaining the Way would be entirely without basis."
Therefore, Candraprabha!

You should know that when people in the final age hear this mantra and believe and understand it with a profound mind, those individuals will, upon changing their bodies, attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas they will constantly gather the merit of Brahma, and they will encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world and perform immeasurable offerings.
They cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) and reach the far shore of all supernormal powers (abhijñā).

In whatever place they take birth, their bodies are as firm and solid as those of Nārāyaṇa; their lifespan is long and enduring, and their bodies are golden-hued, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa).
They attain the Brahma-voice and possess sovereign majesty and virtue throughout all worlds.
“Good son!
What wise person, seeing such benefits as these, would not accept and uphold them? You should know that such a person has lost a great benefit.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha was filled with immeasurable joy and addressed the Buddha again:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We pray that you grant us a moment of leisure so that we may further inquire as to the method for this Great Compassionate Secret Treasury of Dharanis.”
"How should it be received and upheld?
We only pray that you will explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the great assembly, his countenance relaxed and a smile upon his lips, as he praised Candraprabha, saying:
“Excellent, Great Being!
You are able to ask about this matter.”
"Listen with single-minded attention; I shall explain it for you.
The Buddha said to Candraprabha:

"If there are humans or devas who desire to receive and practice this Dharma-gate of my great compassion, those persons should, on the eighth or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, bathe in fragrant water, anoint themselves with various exquisite perfumes, wear pure white garments, and eat the three white foods—namely milk, curd, and rice (or as some say, barley)—while giving rise to a heart of sorrowful pity and vowing to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings."

At the time when the sun rises in the east, or during the full moon at night, in a pure place or on an open ground under the moonlight, one should prepare a maṇḍala of fragrant water three cubits in size as the ritual site; smear the ground with fragrant mud and remove all impurities and rough stones.
The altar shall have four gates; if performed at sunrise, it should be made as a square altar.
If performed during the height of the moonlit night, it should be made in the shape of a full moon, requiring four bowls of milk to be placed at its four corners.
Furthermore, four vases filled with scented water should be placed at the four gates, with seasonal grasses, wood, and flowers of five colors arranged upon their mouths.
Five incense burners are required, arranged at the four corners with one burner placed in the center.
Furthermore, a single lamp—using ghee as its fuel—is to be placed upon the central seat.
Furthermore, take four bowls and fill them with flowers, water, and cooked non-glutinous rice.
In the center of the altar, construct a lotus seat adorned with variegated colored fabrics; spread these upon its pedestal and install there an image of the Buddha or an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Yama and others are stationed at this gate, while the Lord of Devas and others are stationed at the eastern gate; this is a brief description.
It is adorned with various banners and canopies, reflecting one another in a magnificent display.
For incense, one may only use *agaru*—in Chinese, *shen-shui-hsiang* (sandalwood).
Having performed the ritual mudrās according to the rules, the practitioner proceeds to the western gate, facing south, and places a brazier before his seat, burning upright pieces of charcoal.
First, take ghee, curd, and honey, and mix them together in a vessel.

The practitioner first invites the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the great stages, the Vajras, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits; then, with the mind focused and undistracted, they contemplate the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings in the six realms of existence, just as previously described.
Having seen this, one weeps with intense grief, desiring to rescue and protect them.

One further imagines oneself mounting a precious lotus pedestal and flying to that place, massaging their bodies while tears flow like rain, wishing to extinguish the fire. Accompanied by further sobbing and choking sobs, the pain pierces to the very marrow of the bones. If the mind is not in accord [with this visualization], one should imagine all hungry ghosts as being one's own beloved father, wife, or child.
Having performed this visualization fourteen times, one immediately attains within meditative concentration the stage of being the Tathāgata’s most beloved only son.
Emerging from contemplation with this realization, one faces the east and invokes all hungry ghosts of the ten directions.
Having recited this invocation mantra fourteen times, one should further visualize that all spirits fill Jambudvīpa, and then open their throats so that they may attain liberation.
Then, one takes the scented water, milk-rice, incense, flowers, and so forth within the mantra-altar, uses the food-mantra to consecrate them, and returns them to their original places.
At that time, the practitioner takes a handful of curd, recites the food-bestowing mantra three times, and throws one portion into the fire.

When this had been fulfilled a thousand times, at that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts from the ten directions gathered there, crowding together without any gaps between them, joyfully partaking of food and drink.
He immediately manifests his body and speaks with the practitioner; according to the practitioner’s inclinations, he bestows everything upon them without opposition.
The practitioner then provides instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy, causing them to attain liberation.

At that time, the Buddhas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions will praise the practitioner from afar and further bestow upon them the distant prediction of Bodhi. All Bodhisattvas will rejoice and cherish them with affection, while all devas and nāgas will each bring incense, flowers, necklaces, and various kinds of music to offer to the practitioner from afar.

By the power of the practitioner’s spiritual discipline, without rising from their seat, they immediately attain hundreds of thousands of nayutas of dharani-doors and hundreds of thousands of kotis of samadhi-doors.
Good son! To state the essentials:

in this present body, fire cannot burn such a person, water cannot drown them, poison cannot harm them, and blades cannot wound them. When they change seats and receive a new body, they immediately attain the stage of a Tathāgata as one of the Ten Abodes.
The Buddha told Candraprabha:
"This is called the 'Dharma of the Great Maṇḍala for Bestowing the Flavor of Ambrosia.
If one wishes to swiftly attain the stage of the Sole Son (Ekaputrabhūmi), samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and so forth, as well as Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one must enter the great maṇḍala."
"If for some reason it is difficult and you cannot accomplish it, simply practice according to the Dharma as explained above, and all will be successfully realized.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candraprabha:
"This dharani-gate was previously taught by all Buddhas; [It is now being revealed for the sake of all beings. "
I now likewise proclaim this, for the benefit of humans and devas.
If there are those who have faith and delight, and who hear and uphold such a mantra,
listen to its merits as I shall now briefly describe them:
If, throughout a thousand billion kalpas, one has extensively committed unwholesome deeds,
by reciting and upholding this mantra, one can purify them within seven days;
likewise, the various merits accumulated by a bodhisattva over billions of kalpas—
By reciting and upholding this mantra, one will be victorious within seven days.
You should know that the dharmas of all Buddhas involve inconceivable skillful means;
only those who have attained them can truly understand, for the Buddha’s word is non-dual.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, saying: "Good son,
you should know that the merits of this person are inexhaustible, even were one to speak of them."
You should keep this in mind and uphold it according to the Dharma. Why is this?
In various sūtras, I have taught that among both worldly and world-transcending causes, the field of compassion is specifically declared to be the foremost.
Furthermore, Candraprabha!
At one time, I taught the bhikṣus:
"If a person, with a heart of deep reverence, offers me food and drink, but before giving it to me, turns it over instead to give to a dog, I praise that person for attaining immeasurable merit."
"Therefore, Candraprema!

Although one may give to arhats and pratyekabuddhas and receive their retribution in the present life, it is limited and measurable; one shall obtain only the fruit of rebirth among humans and devas for five hundred kalpas."
If one gives even a single morsel of food to a hungry ghost, the merit of that person is itself bodhi; since bodhi is immeasurable, their merit and lifespan are likewise immeasurable.
Listen attentively now; I shall further explain for you the functions and effects of this dhāraṇī:

"If there are heavy sins, evil karmas, or accumulated obstructions that are difficult to eliminate, one should daily consecrate milk porridge with this mantra and offer it to the hungry ghosts (preta). After seven days have been completed, all sinful obstructions will be extinguished without remainder."

Furthermore, there is another method: if a person encounters a severe illness or various afflictions caused by spirits, they should prepare three vessels of flour porridge, recite the mantra over them seven times, and offer them to the hungry ghosts in a desolate wilderness. By doing so for two weeks, the pain and illness encountered will be immediately cured.

Furthermore, if within a kingdom the poison of evil karma spreads, causing epidemics among the people and untimely deaths among livestock, one should construct a fire pit. Taking *sālipiṣpa* seeds (translated in Chinese as white mustard seeds), mixed with ghee, honey, and other substances, one should summon the *bhūtakas* and others. Then, taking a handful at a time, reciting the mantra once for each, one should cast them into the fire. Doing this one hundred and eight times each day for seven days, the malevolent spirits will rejoice, withdraw their evil poisons, and diseases and afflictions will be extinguished.

Furthermore, if anyone should encounter malicious gossip or verbal strife, one should prepare honey-water, recite the mantra over it seven times, and sprinkle it in the four directions; all such verbal strife will naturally be extinguished.

Furthermore, if there should be an enemy harboring a vengeful heart who intends to plot one's harm, one should at dawn prepare delicious food and drink for the various ghosts and spirits, calling out the name of that enemy; these hungry ghosts will then cause that person to encounter misfortune and calamity in advance.

Furthermore, there is another method: during an era of famine, one should recite the mantra over the five grains, milk, curd, and so forth, one hundred and eight times, and cast them into a deep pool; thus, the people of the land will immediately attain abundance and joy.

Furthermore, there is another method: if one wishes to perform the *siddhikṛtya*, one should take cow’s ghee, milk, curd, and so forth, face this direction, recite the mantra over them one thousand times, and offer them to the hungry ghosts, calling out, "Śvetidhavalā and the others!
Take that for me!"
"He will then come immediately; if you wish for him to depart, call for him to take it away and he will do so.

Furthermore, there is another method: if you wish to cause various kinds of wealth and treasures to be brought forth, prepare food as described above and recite the mantra ten thousand times. Then, calling his name and speaking to him, gold, silver, and the seven precious jewels will immediately arrive to be bestowed upon the practitioner."

Furthermore, there is another method: take husked non-glutinous rice, ghee, honey, and so forth; pinch them with one's fingers while reciting the mantra, burning one portion for each repetition until it is completed one thousand and eight times. One will certainly obtain great wealth, and all that is sought shall be fulfilled as desired.

Furthermore, there is another method: if one wishes to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the practitioner should daily offer food and drink to the hungry ghosts (*preta*) for a full hundred days; thus, it will be fully accomplished.

Furthermore, according to another method, if one desires to seek the prolongation of one's lifespan, by performing the aforementioned rite for a full hundred days, one will immediately attain longevity.

Furthermore, according to another method, if one desires that one’s physical appearance, strength, and beauty be such that all who see them rejoice, one should make offerings to the hungry ghosts (preta) for a full hundred days; one will certainly obtain one's wish.
Thus, to speak briefly, if one applies the appropriate remedy with a focused mind to every pursuit, every kind of misfortune, and every affliction, all shall be overcome.
Therefore, I have now spoken only in brief.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candraprabha, saying:
"This dhāraṇī sūtra is inconceivable; even if one were to spend a full kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, speaking of its merits, one could never exhaust them."
If, in a future age, one is able to uphold this sutra, you should know that such a person has already effectively gathered twenty kinds of great masses of merit.
What are these twenty?
First, in the present life, they will not be afflicted by hunger, thirst, poverty, illness, or calamities that distress the body and mind.
Second, whatever food people eat, whether it be delicious or not, shall all become supreme flavor for them.
Third, wherever such a person enters upon a wilderness path, insects, poisons, or even compounded herbal medicines shall never be able to harm them.
Fourth, ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, malevolent demons, and *wangliang* will regard that person as they would a Buddha;
fifth, all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and dragon deities will protect that person as they would their own pupils;
sixth, whatever pestilential diseases that person may have—whether caused by karma or external conditions—will be unable to approach their body.
Seventh, that person’s lifespan will increase; they will sleep in peace and awaken with clarity; and they will encounter auspiciousness in all their affairs.
Eighth, when that person traverses narrow wildernesses where water and grass are scarce, these will naturally become sufficient for their needs.
Ninth, that person’s countenance will be serene and joyful, their skin and body will be radiant, and they will be free from any unsightly complexion.
Tenth, such a person will constantly encounter virtuous friends, even to the point that Bodhisattvas manifest as their companions.
Furthermore, first, such a person will always be born in the future into a Kṣatriya royal family;
second, such a person will be endowed with physical beauty, strength, longevity, happiness, and eloquence.
Third, such a person will always be born in the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
fourth, wherever such a person may be, hidden treasures will spontaneously appear;
fifth, such a person will constantly receive the respect and service of others.
Sixth, none shall be able to seize whatever wealth and treasures that person possesses;
seventh, all that the person intends and desires shall be fully realized;
eighth, that person shall not be born during an eon of famine or calamity.
Ninth, they are constantly reborn in the heavens, experiencing noble and supreme bliss;
tenth, they are always sustained by the joy of the Dharma and the rapture of dhyāna, free from hunger and thirst.
These constitute the twenty kinds of great accumulations of merit.
"Good son! This dhāraṇī possesses sovereign majestic power.
If one recites it while looking at a person who is hungry and thirsty, that person will immediately become satiated."
If by reciting mantras over a withered tree, it can still sprout branches,
why would sentient beings not receive its blessings through such recitation?
For this reason, I now earnestly state this three times, entrusting it to you.
"You should remember and uphold this, and preach it for the sake of sentient beings; do not let it be forgotten.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, having heard this method of skillful means from the Buddha, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately scattered *vaidūrya* maṇi jewels, necklaces, and various flowers and incense over the Buddha.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
“O Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird,
Through manifold skillful words and phrases, You reveal and teach the nectar-like Dharma.”
Because you wish to utterly subdue the vast mountains of karma,
you have earnestly entrusted me with this gateway of skillful means.
Relying upon the Buddha’s solemn teaching, I am capable of widely disseminating it.
“I only pray that within the Dharma, the grass shall again become a *lu*.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the Vajrapāṇis, Śakra, Brahmā, the four guardians, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, having heard the Tathāgata’s praise and exposition of this “Amṛtarasa Dhāraṇī of the Kinnarapila,” were all filled with joy and respectfully practiced according to his instructions.

The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Divine Incantation of the Ambrosial Flavor for Bestowing upon Hungry Ghosts. Namo *buburi* (1) *tathāgatāya* (2) *oṃ* (3) *sarvabhūtakarāya* (4) *āgaccha* (5) *svāhā*. The ritual method for this incantation:
Stand upright and form a cross with both feet.
First, with the left hand, hold it palm upward between the knees, forming the *abhaya-mudrā* (gesture of fearlessness).
Next, with the right hand, place the thumb inside the palm and grasp the four fingers together, holding them against the earring at the right ear, moving it back and forth with the *mukuta-mudrā*.
Immediately, he recited the sublime words three times.

At that moment, all the hungry ghosts and the thirty-six classes of spirits gathered around the person reciting the mantra; with palms joined, they gazed up at the practitioner who was observing them.

If any son or daughter of good family, whether a youth or a maiden, upholds, recites, and studies these sublime words of this dhāraṇī, they shall manifestly practice the ten accumulations of merit in this very life.

What are the ten? First, one cannot be struck by poison; second, venomous snakes dare not sting; third, blades and weapons cannot cause harm; fourth, kings and officials dare not become angry with one; fifth, all people love and respect one; sixth, devas and nāgas constantly follow to protect one; seventh, clothing and food are entirely abundant; eighth, one’s countenance is upright and handsome; ninth, one is forever free from the fear that makes the hair stand on end; tenth, one does not receive a body in the three miserable realms.
Oṃ bupuri gatri tathāgatāya. Regarding the ritual method for the mudrā of this seal:
it follows the ritual method for the summoning seal mentioned above.

Standing with both feet together, join the ten fingers in *añjali*; let the tips of the thumbs touch one another, leaving a space of one inch between them, and open the wrists to place them against the heart.
This is called "The Dharani Method of the Great Compassionate Heart Wheel.
When forming this mudrā, recite the sublime words seven times.
At that time, visualize a crystal maṇi jewel atop the mudrā emitting crystal light that touches all the hungry ghosts, causing all fierce fires to cease burning entirely.
This crystal light enters the mouths of the various *pretas*; their smoke-choked throats all obtain free passage for breath, and they are freed from all suffering and affliction.
*Namo surūpāye tathāgatāya svāhā*. The ritual procedure for the mudrā:
sit in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), according to the sitting method of a Cakravartin king.
First, with the right hand, assume the posture of supporting the neck at a distance of about one cun from it, resting the elbow upon the right knee.
Next, extend the five fingers of the right hand upward and sideways, letting them hang over the right knee in the manner of offering breast-milk.

When forming this mudrā, recite the sublime mantra seven times while visualizing white milk-like nectar emerging from the tips of the ten fingers of the left hand; its color surpasses that of white silver, flowing forth without ceasing.
All these spirits opened their mouths to receive the milk, and each was fully satisfied.
As for those who made this vow, that son of good family shall, in his present body, obtain sixteen kinds of merit.

What are these sixteen? First, a long life span; second, a beautiful complexion; third, abundant physical strength; fourth, a mind constantly filled with joy; fifth, unimpeded eloquence; sixth, never having the thought of hunger; seventh, a mouth that is fragrant and pure; eighth, being revered by all people; ninth, being guarded by celestial deities; tenth, piśāca spirits manifesting their forms to provide service; eleventh, freedom from physical ailments; twelfth, possessing majesty and virtue like a king; thirteenth, all wicked people and evil spirits feeling joy upon seeing them; fourteenth, attaining the merit of a Cakravartin King; fifteenth, dreaming of various bodhisattvas and arhats; and sixteenth, the world shaking at the place where one is born.
